lines.x: 'Assistant'? Just tell me straight what you need me to do. It's fine—whatever I don't know, I can learn, as long as you're willing to teach me.

Where I'm from and how I grew up? Isn't all of that on my résumé? I don't mind you asking, there's just genuinely nothing worth telling. Sorry, I'm not good at small talk. Yes, as you say, maybe I'll get used to it someday. But for now, time spent chatting is better spent working.

My scratch paper looks a bit odd? It does. Someone stuck a strange note on my door, and it seemed a waste to throw it out, so I used it to practice my handwriting. Oh, it was an invitation to a social dance? Nothing to be done—I couldn't read what was written on it at the time. Besides, the date on it was last week.

Zelgrad—I was born on its foundations. When I grew up, I took over my parents' work and went on building that city. We raised the collective dormitories ten stories high, and still they never rose above that stone wall. I don't mind that they concealed things and lied. But why did they have to destroy our home?

What I just picked up off the floor? It's nothing, only an empty medicine bottle. How could it be dirty? Medicine is the thing that kills disease. Once they're washed, Grisha and Masha use them as building blocks. I've saved up quite a lot of bottles like this...

Me and Lyudmila? No, you've got it wrong. Calling ourselves 'Reunion' in Zelgrad wasn't her idea. Most people in the city knew little about their claims or their deeds back then. But when your life is on the line, a name that has always been tied to change is enough to become the beginning of change.

There's something I should mention. A while back I did some odd jobs for the Engineering Department, and today I was paid for it. I wasn't sure whether that's within Rhodes Island's rules. Is that so? Then I'll take it back and eat it without worrying. Hm? Not money, of course—a stew that the one called Alanna sent over.

Excuse me. How do you read these words? 'Heart-rending,' 'vow,' 'infatuation,' and 'remorse.' Oh. Thank you. What book am I reading? I just grabbed it from the library. They say it's a romance novel that's popular lately, but I can't understand the people in it, so I can't say for sure.

Just now, as I came in, it struck me that I've been talking more and more in here. Talking is like pouring water out of a kettle—the more you say, the lighter you feel inside. That weightless feeling frightens me, so today I'm leaving the moment the shift ends. But I'll still be here on time tomorrow, Doctor.
Slacking off and dozing on the clock, without even worrying about being told off by the boss... No, wait. This one is the boss.

Hello. I'm Tanya. Lyudmila told me I could find work here, and get the children treated at the same time. Yes—those are my little brothers and sisters. All of you, come over and say hello to the Doctor.
Does it have to be done this way? I'm only checking. I can do these things. Whether they're kind or cruel has nothing to do with it.

Let go, Grisha, this isn't a toy. Masha, please, hand me that ribbon. Fine, you can sleep with the medal on tonight, as long as the Doctor allows it. My apologies, Doctor—they wouldn't stop pestering me to come to the promotion ceremony.
How much improvement does this medal bring? No, I don't mean my wages or my medicine ration. What I'm asking is: once I've accepted this medal, will I be able to do more, and save more people?
As you say.
I'll do my best.
Steady hands, quick legs, a clear head.
Deep breath. Don't let your hands shake. Aim before you strike.
Me?
Yes, I'm ready.
Anywhere's fine.
You decide.
That's all the strength you have? Weaker than a child.
A wound like this? I hardly noticed.
'Surrender'? Do you take everyone for a fool?
'Drop your weapons'? How is that any different from handing over your life?
What is it? Are you shaken now that it's over, or relieved? Haha... I don't know what I'm laughing at either.
However noble a sacrifice may be, I would rather there were fewer of them. You protected us. You did well.
I only want to save one more. Whether we still have a chance to try again is yours to decide. I'll wait for your call.
Am I willing to accept this? ...Of course not.
A very spacious bed. But I'm at the ward every night keeping watch, so I won't be using it. A shame.
You startled me. Impressive.
Do you enjoy watching other people work? I don't mind—you won't get in my way. Though it would be even better if you lent a hand now and then.
Arknights.

The colored lights, the ball—all of it is new to me. Thank you for bringing me up here to see it. In a few hours I have to make dinner, pick the children up from class, change my own dressings, and clean the dormitory. Doctor, I'd gladly stay and look at this view with you a while longer, but...
The more of a hurry you're in, the slower you should work. As long as you don't stop, it always gets finished.

I made a cake in the cafeteria oven. Don't take a big bite right away—taste it first. I'm not very good at baking. Back when it was my brother's and sisters' birthdays, a little sugar sprinkled on crustless toast was already something. Sugar isn't scarce now, so my worry is that I got greedy and made it too sweet.

Grisha and Masha are doing well in their literacy class, and the littlest one has left intensive care. Logistics found me some light part-time work as well. Why am I telling you all this? Well—before I came to Rhodes Island I thought of this as nothing but a temporary job. But now I find I want to stay here for good.
